question.text: Suppose that a $3 \times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear: \[ R_2:=R_2+R_1, \qquad R_3:=R_3-5R_1 \] Given that $C$ has the LU factorization $C=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
Applying $R_2:=R_2 + {\color{red}1} \cdot R_1$ and then $R_3:=R_3+ ({\color{red}-5}) \cdot R_1$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

\[ \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ {\color{red}-5}& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_2} \cdot \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ {\color{red}1}& 1 & 0 \\ 0& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_1} \cdot C = U \]

Now, since $E_2E_1C=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 C &= U \\[1ex] E_1 C &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{red}1} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{red}-5} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}-1} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}5} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] C &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}-1} & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}5} & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \cdot U \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -6 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -6 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + 2R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[1ex] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }_{U}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Applying $R_2:=R_2 + ({\color{red}-7}) \cdot R_1$ and then $R_3:=R_3+ {\color{red}5} \cdot R_1$ is equivalent to multiplying $C$ from the left by the following elementary matrices:

\[ \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ 0& 1 & 0 \\ \color{red}5& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_2} \cdot \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0 & 0 \\ \color{red}-7& 1 & 0 \\ 0& 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{E_1} \cdot C = U \]

Now, since $E_2E_1C=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization: \begin{align*} E_2 E_1 C &= U \\[1ex] E_1 C &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{red}-7 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \color{red}5 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] C &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{blue}7 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \color{blue}-5 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] C &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \color{blue}7 & 1 & 0 \\ \color{blue}-5 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \cdot U \end{align*}

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -5 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $L=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 \\ -2 & 2 & -5 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + (-3)R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\ &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -5 \end{bmatrix}& R_3 &:= R_3 + 2R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_2} \cdot E_1 \cdot A \\[2ex] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 A &= U \\[1ex] E_1 A &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the LU Factorization Using Two or More Elementary Row Operations

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 4 & 8 & -1 \\ 6 & 9 & -1 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $l_{21}\cdot u_{33}=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 4 & 8 & -1 \\ 6 & 9 & -1 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + \left(-2\right)R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\ &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 6 & 9 & -1 \end{bmatrix}& R_3 &:= R_3 + (-3)R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_2} \cdot E_1 \cdot A \\[2ex] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_2E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_2$ and $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_2 E_1 A &= U \\[1ex] E_1 A &= E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= E_1^{-1} E_2^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \left( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right) U \\[1ex] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=2, u_{33}=2,$ and $l_{21}\cdot u_{33}=4.$
